Document-Based Question: Civil Liberties and the Home Front in World War I

Directions: Read the two documents below. Then write a well-organized essay addressing the following question: How did the U.S. government's management of the home front during World War I reveal fundamental tensions between national security and the constitutional rights of American citizens?

Your essay must:
— Apply HIPP analysis to both documents
— Construct a clear argument about the tension between security and liberty
— Incorporate outside knowledge of specific home-front policies and their effects
— Evaluate whether the balance struck was justified given the wartime context

---
DOCUMENT 1
Espionage Act, June 15, 1917, Section 3 — Statutes at Large of the United States, public domain:
"Whoever, when the United States is at war, shall willfully make or convey false reports or false statements with intent to interfere with the operation or success of the military or naval forces of the United States or to promote the success of its enemies... shall be punished by a fine of not more than $10,000 or imprisonment for not more than twenty years, or both... Any newspaper, magazine, or other publication... containing any matter advocating or urging treason, insurrection, or forcible resistance to any law of the United States is hereby declared to be nonmailable."

---
DOCUMENT 2
Schenck v. United States, Supreme Court of the United States, March 3, 1919 — public domain (U.S. government document):
"The most stringent protection of free speech would not protect a man in falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic. It does not even protect a man from an injunction against uttering words that may have all the effect of force... The question in every case is whether the words used are used in such circumstances and are of such a nature as to create a clear and present danger that they will bring about the substantive evils that Congress has a right to prevent."
— Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes, writing for the Court
items.stemEs:
Pregunta Basada en Documentos: Libertades Civiles y el Frente Interno en la Primera Guerra Mundial

Instrucciones: Lea los dos documentos a continuación. Luego escriba un ensayo bien organizado que aborde la siguiente pregunta: ¿Cómo reveló la gestión del gobierno de EE. UU. del frente interno durante la Primera Guerra Mundial las tensiones fundamentales entre la seguridad nacional y los derechos constitucionales de los ciudadanos americanos?

Su ensayo debe:
— Aplicar el análisis HIPP a ambos documentos
— Construir un argumento claro sobre la tensión entre seguridad y libertad
— Incorporar conocimiento externo de políticas específicas del frente interno y sus efectos
— Evaluar si el equilibrio alcanzado estuvo justificado dado el contexto bélico

---
DOCUMENTO 1
Ley de Espionaje, 15 de junio de 1917, Sección 3 — Estatutos Generales de los Estados Unidos, dominio público:
"Quien, cuando los Estados Unidos estén en guerra, a sabiendas haga o transmita informes o declaraciones falsas con intención de interferir con la operación o el éxito de las fuerzas militares o navales de los Estados Unidos o de promover el éxito de sus enemigos... será castigado con una multa de no más de $10,000 o prisión por no más de veinte años, o ambas... Cualquier periódico, revista u otra publicación... que contenga cualquier asunto que abogue por o exhorte a la traición, insurrección, o resistencia forzosa a cualquier ley de los Estados Unidos queda por la presente declarada no enviable por correo."

---
DOCUMENTO 2
Schenck v. Estados Unidos, Tribunal Supremo de los Estados Unidos, 3 de marzo de 1919 — dominio público (documento del gobierno de EE. UU.):
"La protección más estricta de la libertad de expresión no protegería a un hombre que falsamente gritara 'fuego' en un teatro y causara pánico. Ni siquiera protege a un hombre de una orden judicial contra pronunciar palabras que puedan tener todo el efecto de la fuerza... La pregunta en cada caso es si las palabras usadas se usan en tales circunstancias y son de tal naturaleza que crean un peligro claro y presente de que producirán los males sustanciales que el Congreso tiene derecho a prevenir."
— Juez Oliver Wendell Holmes, escribiendo para el Tribunal
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (6/6) response argues a specific thesis — such as: 'The Espionage Act (1917) and the Schenck decision (1919) together established a wartime security regime that suppressed legitimate political dissent, disproportionately targeting socialist, labor, and immigrant voices, and the "clear and present danger" standard — while appearing moderate — was applied so broadly as to criminalize anti-war opinion rather than genuine sabotage.' HIPP analysis: Document 1 (Espionage Act) — Historical context: U.S. entry into WWI, April 1917; need to protect military operations and manage public opinion; Intended audience: courts, prosecutors, postal officials; Purpose: criminalize anti-war interference with the military and ban disloyal publications from the mail; Point of view: Congress and the Wilson administration regarded anti-war speech as operationally dangerous to the war effort and the draft. Note the 'nonmailable' provision — this gave Postmaster Albert Burleson the power to effectively silence dissident newspapers by denying mail access. Document 2 (Schenck) — Historical context: Schenck was a Socialist Party official who distributed leaflets arguing the draft violated the 13th Amendment; Intended audience: the legal system and the American public; Purpose: establish a constitutional test for when free speech could be restricted; Point of view: Holmes, a progressive jurist, believed wartime emergencies created genuinely different constitutional conditions. Note the 'fire in a theatre' analogy was about false speech (panic-causing lies), but the standard was applied to political opinion, not lies. Outside knowledge: Eugene V. Debs (sentenced to 10 years under the Sedition Act, 1918); IWW ('Wobblies') suppression; German-language newspaper closures; Abrams v. United States (1919, Holmes dissent warning against overextension); contrast with Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969). Evaluation: the balance was not justified because the Sedition Act (1918) extended the Espionage Act to prohibit any criticism of the war or government, going well beyond legitimate security needs.
items.dokRationale: Student must synthesize across multiple standards and sources, constructing an extended argument that connects US.26, US.25 through evidence-based reasoning requiring sustained analytical writing.
items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (6 points):
6 - Exemplary: Complex, specific thesis addressing both security-liberty tension and evaluation of justification. HIPP of both documents accurately — especially Burleson's postal power (Doc 1) and the fire-in-theatre analogy as applied to political speech rather than false speech (Doc 2). Extensive outside knowledge (Debs, IWW, Abrams dissent, Sedition Act of 1918, Brandenburg v. Ohio). Evaluative conclusion is specific and evidence-supported.
5 - Advanced: Clear thesis. HIPP of both documents. Good outside knowledge. Addresses tension and evaluation but may not achieve full nuance on the 'false speech vs. political opinion' distinction.
4 - Proficient: Clear thesis. Both documents used as evidence. HIPP of at least one document. Some outside knowledge. Coherent argument.
3 - Adequate: Thesis present. Both documents used. Some HIPP elements. Limited outside knowledge.
2 - Developing: Weak thesis. Documents used without HIPP.
1 - Beginning: No thesis. Minimal document use.
0 - No response or completely off-topic.

DOCUMENT ANALYSIS EXPECTATIONS:
— Doc 1 (Espionage Act): Note the 'nonmailable' provision as a censorship mechanism; note the breadth of 'willfully make or convey' — it covers intent broadly; historical context = Committee on Public Information (CPI) and propaganda campaign running simultaneously.
— Doc 2 (Schenck): Note Holmes's theatre analogy is technically about a false statement causing panic, not about political opinion — but the ruling applied the test to political leaflets; note 'clear and present danger' became the dominant First Amendment test until Brandenburg.
KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: Espionage Act (1917) provisions; Sedition Act (1918) — extended to any 'disloyal, profane, scurrilous' language about the government; Postmaster Burleson's postal bans; Eugene V. Debs conviction (June 1918); IWW (Wobblies) prosecutions; Committee on Public Information (George Creel); Liberty Bonds / four-minute men; Abrams v. United States (1919, Holmes dissent); Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) replacing 'clear and present danger' with 'imminent lawless action.'
items.explanationEs:
GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (6 puntos):
6 - Ejemplar: Tesis compleja y específica que aborda tanto la tensión seguridad-libertad como la evaluación de la justificación. HIPP de ambos documentos con precisión — especialmente el poder postal de Burleson (Doc 1) y la analogía del teatro aplicada al discurso político en lugar del discurso falso (Doc 2). Amplio conocimiento externo (Debs, IWW, disidencia Abrams, Ley de Sedición de 1918, Brandenburg v. Ohio).
5 - Avanzado: Tesis clara. HIPP de ambos documentos. Buen conocimiento externo. Aborda la tensión y la evaluación.
4 - Competente: Tesis clara. Ambos documentos usados. HIPP de al menos un documento. Algo de conocimiento externo.
3 - Adecuado: Tesis presente. Ambos documentos usados. Algunos elementos HIPP.
2 - En desarrollo: Tesis débil. Documentos sin HIPP.
1 - Inicial: Sin tesis. Uso mínimo de documentos.
0 - Sin respuesta o completamente fuera de tema.

EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Disposiciones de la Ley de Espionaje (1917); Ley de Sedición (1918); prohibiciones postales de Burleson; condena de Eugene V. Debs (junio 1918); procesamientos de IWW; Comité de Información Pública (George Creel); Abrams v. Estados Unidos (1919, disidencia de Holmes); Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969).

items.stem:
Extended Response: Civil Liberties, National Security, and the Recurring Tension in American History

Using your knowledge of U.S. history, write an extended essay evaluating the following question: How have periods of perceived national security crisis historically led to the suppression of civil liberties in the United States, and what does the pattern established during World War I reveal about the enduring tension between the First Amendment and government power?

Your essay must draw on at least three historical examples, at least two of which must be from the World War I era (US.26 standards), and at least one of which must make a cross-era connection to a different period in U.S. history (such as the Civil War, the Red Scare of the 1920s, World War II Japanese American internment, McCarthyism, or post-9/11 policies). Your argument must present a clear claim about whether the balance struck between security and liberty in these episodes was justified or unjustifiable, provide specific evidence for each example, explain the reasoning connecting your evidence to your claim, and address the long-term constitutional legacy of the precedents set during WWI.
items.stemEs:
Respuesta Extendida: Libertades Civiles, Seguridad Nacional y la Tensión Recurrente en la Historia Americana

Usando su conocimiento de la historia de EE. UU., escriba un ensayo extendido que evalúe la siguiente pregunta: ¿Cómo han llevado históricamente los períodos de crisis percibida de seguridad nacional a la supresión de las libertades civiles en los Estados Unidos, y qué revela el patrón establecido durante la Primera Guerra Mundial sobre la tensión duradera entre la Primera Enmienda y el poder del gobierno?

Su ensayo debe apoyarse en al menos tres ejemplos históricos, al menos dos de los cuales deben ser de la era de la Primera Guerra Mundial (estándares US.26), y al menos uno de los cuales debe establecer una conexión entre eras con un período diferente de la historia de EE. UU. (como la Guerra Civil, el Miedo Rojo de los años 1920, el internamiento japonés-americano en la Segunda Guerra Mundial, el macartismo o las políticas posteriores al 11 de septiembre). Su argumento debe presentar una afirmación clara sobre si el equilibrio alcanzado entre la seguridad y la libertad en estos episodios fue justificado o injustificable, proporcionar evidencia específica para cada ejemplo, explicar el razonamiento que conecta su evidencia con su afirmación, y abordar el legado constitucional a largo plazo de los precedentes establecidos durante la Primera Guerra Mundial.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response makes a specific, defensible claim — such as: 'The pattern established during WWI — in which perceived national security emergencies led to broadly written laws that suppressed legitimate political dissent, targeted minority and dissenting communities disproportionately, and received judicial sanction through deferential standards — recurred across American history and reveals a structural vulnerability in the First Amendment when the government frames speech as an operational threat rather than an ideological disagreement.' WWI examples (at least two): (1) Espionage Act (1917) and its postal prohibition — Postmaster Burleson banned numerous socialist and German-language newspapers from the mail; the practical effect was the silencing of political opposition to the war with no judicial review before the ban; (2) Sedition Act (1918) — extended the Espionage Act to criminalize any 'disloyal, profane, scurrilous, or abusive language' about the government; Eugene V. Debs sentenced to 10 years for an anti-war speech; (3) Schenck v. United States (1919) — Holmes's 'clear and present danger' standard appeared neutral but was applied to criminalize political pamphlets, not actual sabotage; the Court's unanimous deference to Congress in wartime set a precedent for future suppression. Cross-era connection (at least one): WWII — Korematsu v. United States (1944), in which the Supreme Court upheld Japanese American internment using a 'military necessity' standard that echoed the wartime deference of Schenck; 70,000 U.S. citizens lost their liberty based on race, not evidence; OR McCarthyism — the Smith Act (1940) and subsequent Communist prosecutions (Dennis v. United States, 1951) drew directly on the Schenck precedent to criminalize mere membership in the Communist Party; OR post-9/11 — USA PATRIOT Act (2001), warrantless surveillance, and the detention of enemy combatants at Guantanamo Bay echoing the wartime-emergency framing. Constitutional legacy: Schenck's 'clear and present danger' was narrowed by Brandeis/Holmes dissents in Abrams (1919) and Gitlow (1925), further limited in Dennis (1951), and ultimately replaced by Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) which required 'imminent lawless action' — meaning that 60 years of legal evolution were needed to correct the WWI-era precedent.
items.dokRationale: Student must synthesize across multiple standards and sources, constructing an extended argument that connects US.26, US.27 through evidence-based reasoning requiring sustained analytical writing.
items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (4 points):
4 - Exemplary: Specific, defensible claim about the structural pattern of civil liberties suppression in security crises. Two or more WWI examples with specific evidence (Espionage Act, Sedition Act, Schenck). At least one cross-era example with specific evidence and explicit connection back to the WWI precedent (not just a parallel — the student should show how WWI created the legal framework that enabled the later suppression). Constitutional legacy of Schenck addressed specifically, including its eventual replacement by Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969). Well-organized argumentative essay.
3 - Proficient: Clear claim. Two WWI examples and one cross-era example, all with specific evidence. Some connection between WWI precedent and cross-era example. Constitutional legacy mentioned. Well-organized.
2 - Developing: Claim present. Two or three examples, but the cross-era connection may be a parallel (both suppressed speech) rather than a causal link (WWI set the precedent that enabled later suppression). Limited constitutional legacy discussion.
1 - Beginning: Little or no claim. One or two examples. No cross-era connection. No constitutional legacy.
0 - No response or completely off-topic.

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: Espionage Act (1917) — postal prohibition, mail ban on 74 newspapers; Sedition Act (1918) — Debs conviction; Schenck v. United States (1919) — clear and present danger; Abrams v. United States (1919) — Holmes/Brandeis dissent; Gitlow v. New York (1925) — incorporation of First Amendment to states; Dennis v. United States (1951) — Smith Act, Communist Party; Korematsu v. United States (1944) — Japanese American internment; McCarthyism (1950–1954); Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) — replacement standard; USA PATRIOT Act (2001) as modern parallel.
SYNTHESIS EXPECTATIONS: The cross-era requirement elevates this beyond US.26 to connect Unit 3 (WWI) to Unit 6 (WWII/Korematsu), Unit 7 (Cold War/McCarthyism), or Unit 10 (post-9/11); the strongest responses show a causal-legal chain (Schenck → Dennis → Brandenburg) rather than just a thematic parallel.
items.explanationEs:
GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (4 puntos):
4 - Ejemplar: Afirmación específica y defendible sobre el patrón estructural de supresión de las libertades civiles en crisis de seguridad. Dos o más ejemplos de la Primera Guerra Mundial con evidencia específica. Al menos un ejemplo entre eras con evidencia específica y conexión explícita con el precedente de la Primera Guerra Mundial. Legado constitucional de Schenck abordado específicamente, incluyendo su eventual reemplazo por Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969). Ensayo argumentativo bien organizado.
3 - Competente: Afirmación clara. Dos ejemplos de la Primera Guerra Mundial y un ejemplo entre eras, todos con evidencia específica. Alguna conexión entre el precedente de la Primera Guerra Mundial y el ejemplo entre eras. Legado constitucional mencionado.
2 - En desarrollo: Afirmación presente. Dos o tres ejemplos, pero la conexión entre eras puede ser un paralelo en lugar de un vínculo causal. Discusión limitada del legado constitucional.
1 - Inicial: Poca o ninguna afirmación. Uno o dos ejemplos. Sin conexión entre eras.
0 - Sin respuesta o completamente fuera de tema.

EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Ley de Espionaje (1917); Ley de Sedición (1918) — condena de Debs; Schenck v. Estados Unidos (1919); Abrams v. Estados Unidos (1919) — disidencia de Holmes/Brandeis; Gitlow v. Nueva York (1925); Dennis v. Estados Unidos (1951) — Ley Smith, Partido Comunista; Korematsu v. Estados Unidos (1944); macartismo (1950–1954); Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969); Ley USA PATRIOT (2001).
EXPECTATIVAS DE SÍNTESIS: El requisito entre eras eleva esto más allá de US.26 para conectar la Unidad 3 (Primera Guerra Mundial) con la Unidad 6 (Segunda Guerra Mundial/Korematsu), la Unidad 7 (Guerra Fría/macartismo) o la Unidad 10 (post-11 de septiembre).
